noi_dung:
The Six Great Principles of Cultivators

Cultivators must have a Dharma-selecting eye ("Dharma-selecting vision") to discern what is right Dharma and what is deviant dharma. What is right Dharma? No fighting, no greed, no seeking, no selfishness, no self-benefit, no lying. These are the six great principles—cultivators following them will gain right knowledge and right views. Conversely, deviant dharma is fighting, greed, seeking, selfishness, self-benefit, lying. With these six come deviant knowledge and views. This is the crux, the dividing line between the two sides—forward is Right Dharma, backward deviant dharma. We must see this clearly.

Given no deviant knowledge or views, one need only hold samadhi power firm—and demon kings can find no way to disturb us, unable to shake our minds. There is a saying: "Kill the Buddha when a Buddha comes; kill the demon when a demon comes." What does this mean? It only advises us not to cling overmuch to states. Seeing a Buddha come, yet not accepting the image—let alone seeing a demon! Though in many cases such states are previews, most efficacious, still we should not believe in them. What we must believe is precisely the six great principles—no fighting, no greed, no seeking, no selfishness, no self-benefit, no lying. That is the demon-slaying sword, the demon-quelling club.

With right knowledge and views complete, though gods appeared to make offerings and bow in reverence, the cultivator's mind would stay unmoved. Should the mind stir, giving rise to delight, then delight-demons seize the chance to break in, driving the cultivator mad. Should gloom arise, then gloom-demons come to stain the mind with afflictions, or sometimes giving rise to clinging, to arrogance. All these are demons' mischief, robbing the mind of purity.

So meeting any bizarre state, the cultivator should not believe, nor let the mind stir. Believe only in your own wisdom—believing the own-nature can give rise to the myriad dharmas, the own-nature fundamentally pure, fundamentally undefiled, fundamentally not upside down. Then what remains to seek? Wherever there is seeking, there is defilement; having fighting, greed, selfishness, self-benefit, lying is having defilement. Meeting any dharma, we can take those six great principles as our measure—observing: what accords is Right Dharma, what accords not is deviant dharma.

The six great principles can smash the deviant knowledge and views of heavenly demons and outside ways. All the contrivings of heavenly demons and outside ways are of a seeking nature—aimed at fighting, greed, seeking, selfishness, self-benefit, lying—for themselves, not for others. Those are the thoughts of side doors and crooked paths.

The cultivator of the Way must gather merit and foster virtue, yet never cling to what has been done—as the saying goes: "sweep away all dharmas, leave behind all marks"—never saying: "I did this merit, I cultivated thus" or "I reached this state, I have such spiritual powers." Supposing such things exist—examined closely, all are hollow—never believe them, never be caught. Believing in marvels and psychic dharmas, the cultivator can never enter right concentration, right reception (samadhi). Understand: right concentration, right reception are not gained from outside—they must arise from the own-nature. How does the cultivator attain them? Through the skill of returning the light inward, seeking back within oneself (seeking from oneself)—only then are right concentration and right reception accomplished.

The City of Ten Thousand Buddhas is where myriads of sages gather. Yet on all four sides, demon kings wait their chance to slip in. If the cultivator's mind is impure, the head full of discursive thoughts, demon kings seize the opening to sneak in and incite—for instance, making the cultivator predict this and that. If the cultivator then believes these are powers he has gained, he has walked into the trap—becoming the Demon King's kin.

Likewise, hearing some sound, you hastily take it for a voice from empty space. In fact empty space holds no speech—know that: "apart from the mark of speech, apart from the mark of mind following conditions." Suppose you hear empty space's voice—that is only a demonic state, not brought by "Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom." What worth is a trifling scrap of news!

The cultivator's mind must be pure. Crave no power of foresight. Foresight brings nothing good—on the contrary, only trouble, distracting us, scattering focus—and so discursive thoughts tangle and afflictions pile up. Without foresight, you will have no afflictions, the mind unobstructed. The Heart Sutra says: "Because there is no obstruction, there is no fear—far apart from all upside-down dream-like thinking: Ultimate Nirvana." This is precisely the practitioner's goal on the Way of cultivation.
